facility_roles.quote: The Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array (AMANDA) is an optical Cherenkov detector consisting of 677 optical modules arranged in 19 strings frozen ~1.5 km — ~2 km deep in the ice sheet at the geographic South Pole.

intervals.label: AMANDA-A deployment
intervals.note: Austral summer 1993–94; four strings of 20 optical modules at 800–1,000 m, later found too shallow.
intervals.quote: The first phase of the AMANDA array, called AMANDA-A, was installed during the 1993-1994 austral summer.

intervals.label: AMANDA-B4 / B10 / AMANDA-II construction
intervals.quote: In later construction campaigns (AMANDA-B4 in 1995-1996, AMANDA-B10 in 1996-1997, and AMANDA-II in 1998-2000), the AMANDA team deployed strings at depths of 1,500 meters and deeper in search of more transparent ice.

intervals.label: operation
intervals.note: End year from the IceCube timeline (“AMANDA-II operated through 2009”). Start year 1996 is supported by the INSPIRE experiment record (date_started 1996-01-01) and by the timeline statement that on 20 March 2005 AMANDA became part of IceCube “after nine years of operation”. No month-precision start or end is published.
intervals.quote: Nine additional strings were added in 2000, bringing the array to a total of 677 optical modules mounted on 19 separate strings that were spread out in a rough circle with a diameter of 200 meters. AMANDA-II operated through 2009.

intervals.label: data taking ended
intervals.note: The collaboration publishes no decommissioning date; the only statement found is “AMANDA-II operated through 2009”, so the terminal event is recorded at year precision.

name: AMANDA
notes: No collaboration record is created: the AMANDA Collaboration merged into the IceCube Collaboration on 20 March 2005 (“On March 20, 2005, after nine years of operation, AMANDA officially became part of IceCube!”) and collaboration:amanda is not an id this workstream owns.

Conflict: the 2008 AMANDA data-release page says “AMANDA-II has operated from 2000 — 2006” (the span of that 7-year dataset), while the IceCube timeline says “AMANDA-II operated through 2009”. The timeline (later, and about the detector rather than a dataset) is used for the operating interval.
Successor pointers are held by the later entity (experiment:icecube lists AMANDA as its predecessor), per v0.2 A1.

physics_goals.quote: AMANDA, the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array, was built as a proof of concept in the mid 1990s and demonstrated that the extremely clear Antarctic ice was suitable for detecting energetic neutrinos.
physics_goals.value: Demonstrate that deep Antarctic ice can be used as a Cherenkov medium for high-energy neutrino detection

physics_goals.quote: Neutrinos from an extraterrestrial source would be detected similarly and show as an excess over the atmospheric neutrino background.
physics_goals.value: Search for high-energy neutrinos from extraterrestrial sources above the atmospheric-neutrino background

summary.plain: The pioneering telescope that froze light sensors into the ice at the South Pole to catch neutrinos. It proved the idea worked and was later absorbed into its much bigger successor, IceCube.
summary.technical: In-ice Cherenkov neutrino telescope at the South Pole, built 1993–2000 in the stages AMANDA-A, B4, B10 and AMANDA-II; final configuration 677 optical modules on 19 strings at ~1.5–2 km depth. Produced the first high-energy neutrino sky map and set the ice-optics and hot-water-drilling groundwork for IceCube.

unique_capabilities.quote: On March 22, 2001, the initial results from AMANDA came out in Nature . Over 138 days in 1997, AMANDA’s sensors saw 263 high-energy neutrinos, and they produced a map showing the origins of those particles in the sky.
unique_capabilities.value: First large in-ice Cherenkov neutrino telescope; produced the first high-energy neutrino sky map (Nature, 2001)
